notes.meaning: Jesus and His disciples cross the Sea of Galilee to the east shore. Old copies of Mark spell the place name in different ways (Gerasenes, Gadarenes, Gergesenes). Many think these names point to one district, probably a lakeside village near the town of Gadara. Matthew Henry notes that Jesus went through a storm to get here, just to rescue one poor man.

The moment Jesus steps ashore, a man with an "unclean spirit" meets Him. That means an evil spirit, or demon, had taken hold of him. Matthew's Gospel mentions two men. Mark probably tells about the fiercer, better-known one.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: A Catholic commentary passes on an old reading from Bede. The man stands for the non-Jewish peoples later won to Christ by the apostles, and the many demons stand for their many sins.

notes.meaning: The man lived among the tombs, which were caves cut into the rock outside town. Jews saw graves as unclean places. People had tried to hold him with chains and shackles, but he snapped them. His strength was more than a normal person's, because the evil spirit drove him. Matthew Henry sees a picture here of stubborn sinners who break God's law like chains.

Day and night he screamed and cut himself with stones. He frightened others, but he himself suffered terribly. Matthew Henry says the devil is a cruel master who wants people to harm themselves. Adam Clarke adds that this shows what Satan could do if God let him, yet the devil himself is kept on a chain.

The man used to rush at people in rage, but now he runs to Jesus and kneels. Christ's unseen power did what chains could not do. Many older writers say the demons were forced to bow before Jesus as their Judge. Others, like Matthew Henry, think the man himself, freed for a moment, came to Jesus for help.

The demon speaks through the man. It knows exactly who Jesus is: the Son of the Most High God. "I beg You before God" is like making Jesus swear an oath. It is striking that the tormentor now fears being tormented, because the demons know their day of judgment is coming.

Mark explains why the demon cried out. Jesus had already ordered it to leave the man. The spirit's loud protest was its answer to that command. A short delay was allowed so that Christ's power would be shown even more clearly.

Jesus asks the name, not because He needed it, but so everyone could see how many demons there were. A Roman "legion" was an army unit of about six thousand soldiers. Here it simply means a huge number. One leader seems to speak for them all. Matthew Henry reminds us we cannot beat such enemies alone, but we can stand in the Lord's strength.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern writers, such as Barclay, suggest the man may have seen Roman legions do terrible things, and that this shaped how he saw himself.

notes.meaning: One spokesman begs on behalf of the many. They did not want to be sent away from that area. Luke says they feared being sent to the "abyss," a place of confinement. Calvin says they hated losing their chance to harm people. Adam Clarke thinks this mostly non-Jewish area felt like their own territory.

On the hills nearby, a large herd of pigs was feeding. The area is very hilly. Under the Law of Moses, pigs were "unclean" animals that Jews were not to eat. Some think the owners were Jews breaking that law; others think the people there were mostly non-Jews.

The demons ask to be sent into the pigs. Matthew Henry thinks they hoped that destroying the pigs would turn the whole region against Jesus. They did not ask to enter another person, because they knew Jesus would never allow it.

Jesus allows it, and about two thousand pigs rush into the sea and drown. This showed how cruel and destructive demons really are, so people would seek Jesus, who alone can beat them. It also shows that God had set limits on what the demons could do to the man. Without those limits, he too might have died. Matthew Henry adds that there is mercy even in losing property while lives are spared.
The men caring for the pigs ran and told everyone in the town and on the farms. People came out to see for themselves. So they had both the herdsmen's report and their own eyes as proof.

They find the wild man sitting calmly, dressed, and thinking clearly. Everyone knew him, so this change was clear proof of God's power. Their fear was awe, a sense that God was there. But Calvin and others note that this fear soon turned into something darker.
The eyewitnesses told the crowd what had happened to the man and to the pigs. The people now had the full story from those who saw it.

Instead of welcoming Jesus, the people begged Him to leave. They cared more about their lost pigs than about a man set free. Calvin says they saw God's power but feared Him as a Judge, not loving Him as a Father. Jesus took them at their word and left.

As Jesus got into the boat, the healed man begged to go with Him. His grateful heart wanted to stay close to the One who rescued him. He may also have wanted to learn from Jesus, or feared the demons might return.

Jesus said no, and gave him a job instead: go home and tell your own people. His family could rejoice at once, and he could be a witness where Jesus would not go. He was to speak especially of God's mercy, His kindness to someone who did not deserve it. Unlike in Galilee, where Jesus often said to keep quiet, here there was no danger of too much excitement.

The man went beyond his home and told his story all over the Decapolis, a region of ten cities. Notice that Jesus said "the Lord" had done this, and the man told what "Jesus" had done. Everyone was amazed. But Matthew Henry sadly notes that many marveled while few followed.
Jesus crossed back to the west side of the lake, near Capernaum. A big crowd was waiting for Him. Matthew Henry notes that when some reject Christ, others gladly welcome Him.

Jairus was a synagogue leader, a man who ran the affairs of the local place of worship. Few such leaders believed in Jesus. Yet this important man fell at Jesus' feet, humbly honoring Him as greater than He looked.
